etymology: From open and -ly: publicly, without concealment. Webster 1828: publicly; not in private; without secrecy. Our Lord commands secrecy in giving and promises an open reward, and Paul uses the word for the public humiliation of the powers at the cross.
biblical_def: The Sermon on the Mount sets secrecy and openness in a deliberate order: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly (Matthew 6:4). The concealment is the disciple’s work; the publication is God’s, and it is promised. Christ Himself moved differently at different times, and John records a moment of deliberate reserve: when his brethren were gone up, then went he also up unto the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret (John 7:10) — His hour was not yet come, and He would not be managed by relatives urging a public display. Paul uses the word for what the cross did to the hostile powers: having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it (Colossians 2:15) — the imagery is a Roman triumph, the conquered paraded in public. And Peter is careful about the limits of the resurrection appearances: Him God raised up the third day, and shewed him openly; not to all the people, but unto witnesses chosen before of God (Acts 10:40-41).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OPENLY as publicly; not in private; without secrecy; and also plainly, evidently, without disguise or reserve.
webster_full: OPENLY, adv. — Publicly; not in private; without secrecy.
Plainly; evidently; without disguise or reserve.
OPEN, a. — Unclosed; not shut; free of access; public; not concealed.
OPEN, v.t. — To unclose; to set open; to make plain; to reveal or disclose.
Anglo-Saxon open; the adverbial -ly from lic, like.
scriptures: Matthew 6:4
That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.
John 7:10
But when his brethren were gone up, then went he also up unto the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret.
Colossians 2:15
And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.
Acts 10:40
Him God raised up the third day, and shewed him openly;
corruption_summary: Matthew 6 makes concealment the disciple’s duty and publication God’s prerogative, which is the direct opposite of a religious culture built on documented and shared good works.
corruption_paragraphs: Our Lord’s instruction is not that giving should be modest but that it should be hidden — the left hand not knowing what the right does — and the reason He gives is blunt: those who give to be seen of men have their reward, receiving in full and at once the only payment they were after. The modern practice of documenting and circulating one’s charitable acts, whether by a ministry publishing its numbers or an individual posting them, cannot be reconciled with the paragraph merely by pleading good motives, because the passage addresses the practice and not only the heart behind it. Where the giving must be known for administrative reasons, Scripture provides for that too (2 Corinthians 8:20-21); what it forbids is the giving whose visibility is the point.

Colossians 2:15 gives the word its most triumphant use, and the picture is worth recovering because it inverts every appearance at Calvary. To every eye present, the powers had made a public spectacle of Christ; Paul says Christ made the public spectacle of them, spoiling principalities and powers and leading them in triumph. This is the answer to the persistent instinct that the cross was a defeat God afterwards reversed. The Reformed doctrine of the atonement holds the cross itself as the victory — sin borne, wrath satisfied, the accuser disarmed — with the resurrection as its public vindication. Acts 10:40 adds the sober qualification about that vindication: God shewed Him openly, but to chosen witnesses, not indiscriminately, which is why the church rests on apostolic testimony rather than on general spectacle.
roots_summary: Greek en to phanero, in the open, openly; parresia (G3954), boldness, openness of speech; deigmatizo (G1165), to make a public example of; emphanes (G1717), manifest.
roots_lines: Greek en to phanero — in the open; the promised reward of Matthew 6:4.
Greek parresia (G3954) — freedom of speech, openness; not openly in John 7:10 is literally not in parresia.
Greek deigmatizo (G1165) — to make a public example or spectacle of; made a shew of them openly (Colossians 2:15).
Greek thriambeuo (G2358) — to lead in triumph, as a Roman general; the verb of the same verse.
Greek emphanes (G1717) — manifest, visible; shewed him openly (Acts 10:40).
usage: Thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly (Matthew 6:4) — concealment is the disciple’s work, publication is God’s.
Not openly, but as it were in secret (John 7:10) — Christ refusing to be managed into a public display.
He made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it (Colossians 2:15) — the spectacle at Calvary inverted.

etymology: From Latin secretus, set apart, hidden, from secernere, to separate. Webster 1828: privately; not openly; without the knowledge of others. Scripture uses it of a disciple who was afraid, and of an enticement that comes from inside the family.
biblical_def: John names Joseph of Arimathaea with an honesty that spares him nothing and then records what he did: Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, besought Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus (John 19:38). The secrecy is stated as a fault and the courage is stated as a fact; he asked openly for the body of an executed blasphemer at the moment when the public disciples had fled. Martha uses the same word with tenderness: she went her way, and called Mary her sister secretly, saying, The Master is come, and calleth for thee (John 11:28). Not all concealment is cowardice. But Deuteronomy names the most dangerous kind, and its danger is its intimacy: If thy brother, the son of thy mother, or thy son, or thy daughter, or the wife of thy bosom, or thy friend, which is as thine own soul, entice thee secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods (Deuteronomy 13:6). And Laban complains of a departure done by stealth: Wherefore didst thou flee away secretly, and steal away from me? (Genesis 31:27).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SECRETLY as privately; not openly; without the knowledge of others; inwardly; in the heart.
webster_full: SECRETLY, adv. — Privately; not openly; without the knowledge of others.
Inwardly; not apparently or visibly; latently.
SECRET, a. — Properly, separate; hence, concealed from notice; unseen; private; unknown.
SECRET, n. — Something studiously concealed; a thing not discovered.
Latin secretus, from secerno, to separate — the root of discern and secretary.
scriptures: John 19:38

And after this Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, besought Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus: and Pilate gave him leave. He came therefore, and took the body of Jesus.
John 11:28
And when she had so said, she went her way, and called Mary her sister secretly, saying, The Master is come, and calleth for thee.
Deuteronomy 13:6

If thy brother, the son of thy mother, or thy son, or thy daughter, or the wife of thy bosom, or thy friend, which is as thine own soul, entice thee secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, which thou hast not known, thou, nor thy fathers;
Genesis 31:27
Wherefore didst thou flee away secretly, and steal away from me; and didst not tell me, that I might have sent thee away with mirth, and with songs, with tabret, and with harp?
corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 13 locates the gravest danger of apostasy in the closest relationships, which cuts against the assumption that spiritual threat arrives from strangers and hostile outsiders.
corruption_paragraphs: The list in Deuteronomy 13:6 is deliberately intimate and it descends inward: brother, son, daughter, the wife of thy bosom, the friend which is as thine own soul. The enticement to serve other gods is not expected from an enemy but from the person best positioned to be believed, and it comes secretly, in the confidence that intimacy affords. Churches that conceive of doctrinal danger chiefly as an external assault — the hostile culture, the aggressive unbeliever — are watching the wrong door. Paul says the same to the Ephesian elders: of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them (Acts 20:30). The severity of the Mosaic penalty in this chapter is proportioned to the danger, and while the civil penalty belonged to Israel’s theocratic order, the moral warning did not expire with it.

John 19:38 is one of Scripture’s quiet mercies to the fearful. Joseph had been a secret disciple, and John says so without softening it — for fear of the Jews. Yet he is the man who goes to Pilate for the body when the apostles have scattered, and Nicodemus, who first came by night, comes with a hundred pound weight of myrrh and aloes. The two men who acted in the hours after the crucifixion were the two the narrative had marked as timid. This is not a commendation of secrecy; it is a record of what grace does with cowards, and it should make the church slower to write off a believer whose courage has not yet arrived.
roots_summary: Hebrew bassether (from H5643), in secret, secretly; ganab (H1589), to steal, and so to act by stealth; Greek lathra (G2977), secretly, privately; krupto (G2928), to hide.
roots_lines: Greek lathra (G2977) — secretly, privately; Martha calling Mary (John 11:28) and Joseph’s concealed discipleship (John 19:38).
Greek krupto (G2928) — to hide or conceal; the participle behind being a disciple... but secretly.
Hebrew sether (H5643) — a covering, a hiding place; entice thee secretly (Deuteronomy 13:6).
Hebrew ganab (H1589) — to steal; flee away secretly, literally to steal away (Genesis 31:27).
Hebrew suth (H5496) — to entice or incite; the verb of the intimate temptation in Deuteronomy 13:6.
usage: Being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews (John 19:38) — the fault stated, and the courage recorded in the same sentence.
Called Mary her sister secretly (John 11:28) — not all concealment is cowardice.
The wife of thy bosom, or thy friend, which is as thine own soul, entice thee secretly (Deuteronomy 13:6) — the danger is intimacy, not hostility.

etymology: From Latin denegare, to refuse or say no, from de and negare, to deny. Webster 1828: contradicted; refused; disowned. Scripture applies the word to Peter, to the nation, and, most unexpectedly, to a man who fails to provide for his household.
biblical_def: The most famous denial in Scripture is recorded without any softening: But he denied before them all, saying, I know not what thou sayest (Matthew 26:70) — before them all, and the Gospel that reports it most bleakly is Mark, which the church has long held was Peter’s own account. Peter later preaches the same charge to the nation, and the wording is careful: ye denied the Holy One and the Just, and desired a murderer to be granted unto you (Acts 3:14). He knew what the word cost. Paul then applies it in a place no one expects: if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel (1 Timothy 5:8). Denial is not only a word spoken under pressure; it can be a duty left undone at home. And to the church at Philadelphia, the risen Christ names the opposite as the whole of their commendation: thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name (Revelation 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DENY as to contradict; to gainsay; to declare a statement untrue; to refuse to grant; to disown, to renounce or reject; hence DENIED, contradicted, refused, disowned.
webster_full: DENY, v.t. — To contradict; to gainsay; to declare a statement or position not to be true.
To refuse to grant; as, we asked for bread, and it was denied us.
To disown; to refuse to acknowledge; to renounce; as, to deny one’s self.
DENIED, pp. — Contradicted; refused; disowned; renounced.
Latin denegare, from de and nego, to say no — the root of negative.
scriptures: Matthew 26:70
But he denied before them all, saying, I know not what thou sayest.
Acts 3:14
But ye denied the Holy One and the Just, and desired a murderer to be granted unto you;
1 Timothy 5:8
But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
Revelation 3:8
I know thy works: behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it: for thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name.
corruption_summary: 1 Timothy 5:8 calls failure to provide for one’s household a denial of the faith, which is a far stronger claim about domestic duty than most churches are willing to make.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul does not say that neglecting one’s household is inconsistent with the faith or falls short of it; he says the man hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel — worse than an unbeliever, because even unbelievers commonly provide for their own. The context is the church’s care of widows, and the principle is that the family bears the first obligation and the church takes up what the family genuinely cannot. Two errors follow from losing this. The first is the pattern in which a man’s ministry activity is treated as compensating for his household’s neglect, which the qualifications for elder in 1 Timothy 3:4-5 explicitly forbid: he that knows not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God? The second is the assumption that institutional welfare replaces familial duty, which this verse denies.

Peter’s denial is preserved in all four Gospels, and it is worth asking why. The apostle whom the church at Rome regarded as its founder is presented, in the Gospel most closely associated with him, cursing and swearing that he never knew Christ. The early church did not suppress this, which is a mark of the honesty of the record; but the deeper reason is doctrinal. Our Lord had told Peter beforehand that Satan had desired to have him, that He had prayed for him, and that when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren (Luke 22:32). The denial did not surprise Christ and did not sever the man. That is perseverance of the saints exactly as the confession states it: not that the saints never fall grievously, but that they are kept, and restored, by the intercession of Christ.
roots_summary: Greek arneomai (G720), to deny or disown; aparneomai (G533), to deny utterly; epaischunomai (G1870), to be ashamed of; Latin nego, to say no.
roots_lines: Greek arneomai (G720) — to deny, to disown; Peter’s denial (Matthew 26:70), the nation’s (Acts 3:14), and the household’s (1 Timothy 5:8).
Greek aparneomai (G533) — to deny utterly; the word Christ used in foretelling the threefold denial (Matthew 26:34).
Greek apistos (G571) — an unbeliever, an infidel; the comparison in 1 Timothy 5:8.
Greek pronoeo (G4306) — to think of beforehand, to provide; the duty whose neglect is called denial.
Greek tereo (G5083) — to keep or guard; hast kept my word (Revelation 3:8), the opposite of denial.
usage: He denied before them all (Matthew 26:70) — recorded in all four Gospels, and most bleakly in Peter’s own.
He hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel (1 Timothy 5:8) — denial as a duty left undone at home.
Hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name (Revelation 3:8) — the whole commendation of a church with little strength.

etymology: From un- and known. Webster 1828: not known; not discovered or found out; not heard of. Paul finds an altar to an unknown god in Athens and preaches from it, and uses the same word for a tongue nobody can understand.
biblical_def: In Athens Paul takes a pagan inscription as his text: as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you (Acts 17:23). He does not commend the altar; he uses it to establish that the God he preaches is the One they have confessed themselves ignorant of, and then proceeds to the creation, the resurrection, and the command to repent. The word governs Paul’s whole argument about tongues in the assembly: he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him (1 Corinthians 14:2). The chapter’s single criterion is edification, and what cannot be understood cannot edify. Paul also uses it of himself in one of his great paradoxes: As unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and, behold, we live; as chastened, and not killed (2 Corinthians 6:9). And of his own early obscurity: I was unknown by face unto the churches of Judaea which were in Christ (Galatians 1:22).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines UNKNOWN as not known; not discovered or found out; not heard of; and, of persons, not recognized or acquainted with.
webster_full: UNKNOWN, a. — Not known; not discovered or found out.
Not heard of; obscure; as an unknown author.
Greater than is imagined or ascertained; as unknown wealth.
Not having had acquaintance with; as, unknown to the churches by face.
From un-, not, and known, past participle of know.
scriptures: Acts 17:23
For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.
1 Corinthians 14:2
For he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him; howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries.
2 Corinthians 6:9
As unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and, behold, we live; as chastened, and not killed;
Galatians 1:22
And was unknown by face unto the churches of Judaea which were in Christ:
corruption_summary: Acts 17 is regularly read as an endorsement of finding common ground with pagan religion, when Paul quotes the altar and the poets in order to overturn the theology behind them.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s Areopagus address is the standard proof-text for the method that seeks continuity between the gospel and the religions around it, and the speech itself will not support that use. He begins by saying the city is wholly given to idolatry, calls their worship ignorant, denies that God dwells in temples made with hands or is served by men’s hands as though He needed anything, declares that God now commands all men everywhere to repent, and closes with a fixed day of judgment by a Man whom God raised from the dead. The altar and the line from the poets are points of contact used as leverage, not as agreement. Contextualization in Scripture means finding the hearer’s starting place in order to move him; it never means locating a common theology and stopping there. The result at Athens was mockery from some, delay from others, and a few who clave to him and believed.

1 Corinthians 14 supplies the criterion by which the modern charismatic practice of tongues must be assessed, and it is the apostle’s own: edification of the assembly. Paul rules that in the church he would rather speak five words with understanding than ten thousand in an unknown tongue, that not more than two or three should speak and by course, that there must be an interpreter or the speaker keep silence, and that if an unbeliever enters and hears everyone speaking in tongues he will say they are mad. This dictionary holds the cessationist position of the Reformed mainstream on the sign gifts; but even those who do not need only apply Paul’s own regulations to find most contemporary practice unrecognisable. The chapter ends by requiring that all things be done decently and in order.
roots_summary: Greek agnostos (G57), unknown, from a- and ginosko; agnoeo (G50), to be ignorant of; glossa (G1100), a tongue or language.
roots_lines: Greek agnostos (G57) — unknown; the Athenian inscription of Acts 17:23, and the source of English agnostic.
Greek agnoeo (G50) — to be ignorant; whom therefore ye ignorantly worship (Acts 17:23).
Greek glossa (G1100) — a tongue, a language; the subject of 1 Corinthians 14 (the word unknown is supplied by the translators).
Greek oikodome (G3619) — building up, edification; the governing criterion of the chapter.
Greek agnoeo in 2 Corinthians 6:9 — the participle behind as unknown, and yet well known.
usage: TO THE UNKNOWN GOD... him declare I unto you (Acts 17:23) — an altar used as leverage, not as agreement.
He that speaketh in an unknown tongue... no man understandeth him (1 Corinthians 14:2) — what cannot be understood cannot edify.
As unknown, and yet well known (2 Corinthians 6:9) — the apostolic paradox of obscurity and standing.

etymology: From Old French trier, to pick out, to sift. Webster 1828: to examine; to prove by a test; to purify by fire, as metals. In Scripture the word is metallurgical before it is moral: God tries the heart as a refiner tries silver.
biblical_def: The Old Testament’s word for trying is a refiner’s word, and God is its subject. Jeremiah states it as a divine prerogative and an inescapable one: I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings (Jeremiah 17:10) — and the verse before it is the one that says the heart is deceitful above all things. David invites the same examination on himself: Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart (Psalm 26:2). Peter applies the metaphor to persecution and forbids surprise: think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you (1 Peter 4:12). And John gives the church a duty of trying, with an objective standard: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world (1 John 4:1). The command is addressed to ordinary believers, not to specialists.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TRY as to examine; to prove by a test or experiment; to purify or refine, as metals by fire; to examine judicially; to attempt or endeavor.
webster_full: TRY, v.t. — To examine; to make experiment on; to prove by a test.
To purify; to refine; as, to try metals by fire.
To examine judicially; to hear and determine a cause.
To attempt; to endeavor; to make an effort.
Old French trier, to pick out or sift — the root of trial and of the winnowing sense in triage.
scriptures: Jeremiah 17:10
I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.
Psalm 26:2
Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart.
1 Peter 4:12
Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you:
1 John 4:1
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
corruption_summary: 1 John 4:1 commands ordinary Christians to test spiritual claims by doctrine, which is the opposite of the deference that treats a claimed anointing as beyond examination.
corruption_paragraphs: Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God. The command is in the plural and addressed to the whole church, the standard given in the next verse is doctrinal (the confession that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh), and the stated reason is that many false prophets have gone out. Nothing in the instruction defers to the claimant’s power, results, sincerity or anointing. This is the standing answer to the culture — found in the New Apostolic Reformation and wherever prophetic office is claimed — in which questioning a leader is treated as touching the LORD’s anointed. The Bereans were called more noble for searching the Scriptures daily to see whether even Paul’s preaching was so (Acts 17:11), and Paul commended them for it.

Jeremiah 17:9-10 must be kept together. The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? is immediately answered by I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins. The question is not rhetorical despair; it has an answer, and the answer is God. This is the ground of a properly Reformed self-examination, and it explains why David can pray to be tried rather than dreading it. A man cannot audit his own heart reliably — that is precisely what verse 9 denies — so he submits it to One who can, and asks to be shown. The modern practice of introspection as self-diagnosis attempts what Jeremiah says is impossible; the psalmist’s practice of inviting divine examination attempts what God says He does.
roots_summary: Hebrew bachan (H974), to examine or prove, as metal; tsaraph (H6884), to refine or smelt; nasah (H5254), to test; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test and approve; peirasmos (G3986), a trial.
roots_lines: Hebrew bachan (H974) — to examine, to try as metal is assayed; I try the reins (Jeremiah 17:10) and try my reins and my heart (Psalm 26:2).
Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to smelt or refine; the refiner’s image behind the whole word-group (Zechariah 13:9).
Hebrew kilyah (H3629) — the reins or kidneys, taken as the seat of the inmost affections.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test with a view to approval; try the spirits (1 John 4:1).
Greek purosis (G4451) — a burning, a fiery ordeal; the fiery trial which is to try you (1 Peter 4:12).
usage: I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins (Jeremiah 17:10) — the answer to the question the verse before it asks.
Examine me, O LORD, and prove me (Psalm 26:2) — a man submitting what he cannot audit himself.
Try the spirits whether they are of God (1 John 4:1) — addressed to ordinary believers, with a doctrinal standard.

etymology: From free and -ly: without cost, without constraint, liberally. Webster 1828: at liberty; without constraint; gratuitously. The word marks the manner of God’s giving from the first command in Eden to the last invitation in Revelation.
biblical_def: The first word God speaks to man about the garden is a permission, and it is generous before it is restrictive: Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat (Genesis 2:16). The prohibition follows in the next verse and concerns one tree; the liberty is stated first and covers everything else. That order is worth noticing, because the serpent will invert it in Genesis 3:1. The word then carries the doctrine of justification: Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:24) — the Greek adverb means as a gift, without cause in the recipient, the same word rendered without a cause in John 15:25. Our Lord sets the manner of ministry to match the manner of receiving: freely ye have received, freely give (Matthew 10:8). And Scripture closes with the invitation in the same terms: whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely (Revelation 22:17).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FREELY as at liberty; without constraint or restraint; without necessity; liberally; generously; gratuitously; without purchase or cost.
webster_full: FREELY, adv. — At liberty; without vassalage, slavery or dependence.
Without constraint, restraint or compulsion; of one’s own accord.
Plentifully; in abundance; as, to eat freely.
Without scruple or reserve; also, gratuitously, without purchase or cost.
From free, Anglo-Saxon freo, and the adverbial -ly.
scriptures: Genesis 2:16
And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat:
Romans 3:24
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
Matthew 10:8
Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils: freely ye have received, freely give.
Revelation 22:17
And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
corruption_summary: Romans 3:24 says justification is freely given — as a gift, without cause in the receiver — which is the precise word Rome’s doctrine of infused righteousness and merit cannot accommodate.
corruption_paragraphs: The Greek adverb in Romans 3:24 is dorean, meaning as a gift, gratuitously, and the same word is used in John 15:25 for hating Christ without a cause. Justification, then, is without cause in the justified — there is nothing in the sinner that occasions it. This is the exact point of the Reformation controversy. Trent anathematized the doctrine that a man is justified by faith alone and that the righteousness by which he is justified is Christ’s imputed to him rather than his own infused and cooperated with; and the whole apparatus of merit, satisfaction and indulgence follows from denying dorean. The Protestant answer is not that works do not matter but that they are the fruit of justification and never its cause. Grace ceases to be grace the moment a cause in the receiver is admitted (Romans 11:6).

Genesis 2:16 rewards attention for the order in which God speaks. The liberty is announced first and is comprehensive — every tree of the garden — and one prohibition follows. When the serpent opens his mouth in Genesis 3:1 he reverses this: Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden? The first recorded temptation is a misrepresentation of God’s generosity as restriction, and every temptation since has carried some form of the same suggestion, that obedience is a narrowing and God is holding out. The doctrine to hold against it is stated in the same chapter: God gave everything and withheld one thing, and the one thing was withheld for the good of the man who was given all the rest.
roots_summary: Hebrew akol tokel, an emphatic infinitive absolute, eating thou mayest eat; Greek dorean (G1432), as a gift, gratuitously; charis (G5485), grace.
roots_lines: Hebrew akol tokel — the infinitive absolute doubling the verb for emphasis; thou mayest freely eat (Genesis 2:16).
Greek dorean (G1432) — as a gift, gratuitously, without cause; justified freely by his grace (Romans 3:24).
Greek charis (G5485) — grace, unmerited favour; the companion noun in the same clause.
Greek apolutrosis (G629) — redemption, a ransoming; the means through which the free justification comes.
Greek thelo (G2309) — to will or desire; whosoever will (Revelation 22:17).
usage: Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat (Genesis 2:16) — the liberty stated first, and comprehensive.
Being justified freely by his grace (Romans 3:24) — dorean, without cause in the receiver.
Freely ye have received, freely give (Matthew 10:8) — the manner of ministry matched to the manner of receiving.

etymology: From haste, of Germanic origin through Old French haste. Webster 1828: quick; speedy; also, rash, precipitate, passionate. In the wisdom literature it is nearly always a fault, and the faults it names are three: hasty anger, hasty words, and hasty gain.
biblical_def: Ecclesiastes locates anger’s problem in its speed and then in its lodging: Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools (Ecclesiastes 7:9). The warning is not against anger as such — Scripture commands a righteous kind — but against the anger that arrives quickly and then takes up residence. Proverbs makes hasty speech worse than folly: Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him (Proverbs 29:20). That is a startling comparison; the fool at least may be taught, while the man who speaks before thinking has a settled habit that instruction cannot reach. Proverbs also names hasty gain and predicts its end: The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want (Proverbs 21:5). And Daniel uses the word of a royal decree issued in a rage: Why is the decree so hasty from the king? (Daniel 2:15) — Nebuchadnezzar had ordered every wise man in Babylon killed.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HASTY as quick; speedy; opposed to slow; also precipitate, rash, passionate; easily excited to wrath; and of things, early ripe.
webster_full: HASTY, a. — Quick; speedy; opposed to slow; as, hasty in his motions.
Precipitate; rash; opposed to deliberate; as a hasty resolution.
Passionate; easily excited to wrath; irritable.
Early ripe; forward; as the hasty fruit before the summer (Isaiah 28:4).
From haste, Old French haste, of Germanic origin.
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 7:9
Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools.
Proverbs 29:20
Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him.
Proverbs 21:5
The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want.
Daniel 2:15
He answered and said to Arioch the king's captain, Why is the decree so hasty from the king? Then Arioch made the thing known to Daniel.
corruption_summary: Scripture treats hasty speech as a settled fault worse than folly, which a communication culture built on immediate public reaction is structurally unable to accommodate.
corruption_paragraphs: Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him. The judgment is severe and its logic is worth following: a fool may be instructed, but the man whose words outrun his thought has a fixed habit that keeps him from ever being taught, since he has committed himself publicly before he has understood. Every technology of instant response rewards exactly this trait and punishes the opposite. James gives the proportion — swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath (James 1:19) — and it is precisely inverted by a medium that measures value in speed and volume. This is not a complaint about novelty; Proverbs was written long before any of it. It is an observation that the habit Scripture calls worse than folly has become a professional skill.

Ecclesiastes 7:9 needs its qualification stated or it becomes unbiblical. Scripture does not forbid anger: God’s wrath is holy, Christ looked round about on them with anger (Mark 3:5), and Ephesians 4:26 says Be ye angry, and sin not. What the Preacher forbids is anger that is hasty in arriving and then resteth in the bosom — that is, settles and stays. The same verse in Ephesians supplies the limit: let not the sun go down upon your wrath. The therapeutic account, which treats anger as a neutral emotion needing only healthy expression, and the pietistic account, which treats all anger as sin, both miss what Scripture actually regulates: its speed, its cause, and its lodging.
roots_summary: Hebrew bahal (H926), to be alarmed or hurried; uts (H213), to press or hasten; chatsaph (Aramaic H2685), urgent or harsh; kaas (H3708), vexation or anger.
roots_lines: Hebrew bahal (H926) — to be dismayed or hurried; be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry (Ecclesiastes 7:9).
Hebrew uts (H213) — to press, to be urgent; every one that is hasty only to want (Proverbs 21:5).
Aramaic chatsaph (H2685) — urgent, harsh, peremptory; the decree of Daniel 2:15.
Hebrew kaas (H3708) — vexation, provocation, anger; what rests in the bosom of fools.
Hebrew cheq (H2436) — the bosom, the fold of the garment; where the fool’s anger takes lodging.
usage: Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools (Ecclesiastes 7:9) — the speed and the lodging are both the fault.
Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him (Proverbs 29:20) — the fool can still be taught.
Why is the decree so hasty from the king? (Daniel 2:15) — a rage that had condemned every wise man in Babylon.

etymology: From Middle English ofte, Anglo-Saxon oft: frequently, many times. Webster 1828: frequently; many times; not seldom. Malachi records what those who feared the LORD did often, and Christ tells Jerusalem how often He would have gathered her.
biblical_def: Malachi records a small and unofficial practice and then records heaven’s response to it: Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name (Malachi 3:16). In a chapter about a nation saying it is vain to serve God, a remnant simply talked to each other frequently, and a book was written. Our Lord uses the word in His lament over the city: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets... how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not! (Matthew 23:37). Paul makes it the governing adverb of the Supper: as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come (1 Corinthians 11:26). And he writes to Timothy about a recurring bodily complaint with entirely practical counsel: use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities (1 Timothy 5:23).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OFTEN as frequently; many times; not seldom; and as an adjective in older usage, frequent, as in thine often infirmities.
webster_full: OFTEN, adv. — Frequently; many times; not seldom.
OFTEN, a. (obsolete except in Scripture) — Frequent; as, thine often infirmities.
OFTENTIMES, adv. — Frequently; often; many times.
OFT, adv. — The older and shorter form, retained chiefly in poetry.
Anglo-Saxon oft, frequently.
scriptures: Malachi 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
Matthew 23:37

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!
1 Corinthians 11:26
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
1 Timothy 5:23
Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities.
corruption_summary: 1 Timothy 5:23 is the standing embarrassment of teetotal absolutism, and Malachi 3:16 is the standing rebuke to the assumption that only organized ministry counts.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul tells Timothy to stop drinking only water and to use a little wine for his stomach and his frequent infirmities. The verse does not license drunkenness — Scripture condemns that repeatedly and requires elders not to be given to wine — but it does forbid the position that abstinence is itself a mark of holiness, since an apostle here prescribes the opposite to a young minister. The 1689 Confession’s teaching that God alone is Lord of the conscience applies directly: where Scripture has not bound, no man may bind. A believer may abstain for reasons of conscience, testimony, or the weakness of a brother, and Romans 14 protects him in it; what he may not do is make his abstinence the rule for others, which is precisely the reversal Romans 14 also forbids.

Malachi 3:16 is easy to pass over and is worth dwelling on. The chapter records a nation grown cynical — It is vain to serve God — and then a group who feared the LORD and simply spake often one to another. There is no programme, no office, no public act; there is frequent conversation among people who thought upon His name. The response is that the LORD hearkened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written. Where a church measures spiritual seriousness by attendance at organized events, this verse describes an activity it cannot count, and heaven wrote it down. The Puritan practice of conference — believers meeting to speak of the things of God — was a deliberate recovery of exactly this text.
roots_summary: Hebrew az with the frequentative sense, then... often; Greek posakis (G4212), how often; hosakis (G3740), as often as; puknos (G4437), frequent.
roots_lines: Greek posakis (G4212) — how often, how many times; the Lord’s lament over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37).
Greek hosakis (G3740) — as often as, whenever; the governing adverb of the Supper (1 Corinthians 11:26).
Greek puknos (G4437) — frequent, often recurring; thine often infirmities (1 Timothy 5:23).
Hebrew zikkaron (H2146) — a memorial or remembrance; a book of remembrance (Malachi 3:16).
Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear or revere; those who feared the LORD and spake often.
usage: They that feared the LORD spake often one to another (Malachi 3:16) — no programme and no office, and a book was written.
How often would I have gathered thy children together... and ye would not! (Matthew 23:37) — the lament of a rejected Saviour.
As often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup (1 Corinthians 11:26) — the Supper as a repeated showing forth.

etymology: From Middle English twies, from Anglo-Saxon twiges, the genitive of twa, two. Webster 1828: two times; once and again; doubly. Jude coins one of Scripture’s most alarming phrases with it, and Job uses it for the persistence of a God who speaks unheard.
biblical_def: Jude’s description of false teachers piles image on image and ends with a phrase that has no parallel: clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots (Jude 1:12). Twice dead — dead in the trespasses and sins common to all men, and dead again in an apostasy that has abandoned the profession once made. The tree is not merely barren but uprooted. Job’s friend Elihu uses the word for divine persistence against human dullness: For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not (Job 33:14) — the failure is in the perceiving, not the speaking. The Pharisee in the parable offers his frequency as his credential: I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess (Luke 18:12), and goes down to his house not justified. And Kings records a king repeatedly saved by a prophet’s warning: the king of Israel sent to the place which the man of God told him and warned him of, and saved himself there, not once nor twice (2 Kings 6:10).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TWICE as two times; once and again; and also doubly, in twofold measure or degree.
webster_full: TWICE, adv. — Two times.
Doubly; in twofold degree or quantity; as twice the amount.
Once and again; repeatedly.
TWICE-TOLD, a. — Related a second time; hence, stale or wearisome.
Anglo-Saxon twiges, from twa, two — the adverbial genitive, as in once and thrice.
scriptures: Jude 1:12

These are spots in your feasts of charity, when they feast with you, feeding themselves without fear: clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots;
For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not.
Luke 18:12
I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.
2 Kings 6:10
And the king of Israel sent to the place which the man of God told him and warned him of, and saved himself there, not once nor twice.
corruption_summary: The Pharisee’s I fast twice in the week is a true statement of genuine discipline offered as a ground of acceptance, which is why the parable ends with him unjustified.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing the Pharisee says in Luke 18 is false. He did fast twice a week, beyond what the law required; he did tithe all his possessions; he was not an extortioner or an adulterer. The parable does not expose him as a hypocrite in the sense of a liar — it exposes the ground he stood on. He prayed with himself, thanked God that he was not as other men, and made his record the basis of his standing. The publican, who had no record to offer, smote his breast and asked God to be merciful to him a sinner, and went down to his house justified rather than the other. This is the doctrine of justification in a parable: the ground of acceptance is God’s mercy received by faith, never the believer’s attainment, however real that attainment may be. Real disciplines become deadly the moment they are offered as a claim.

Jude’s twice dead, plucked up by the roots is the sharpest description of apostasy in the New Testament, and it must be read alongside the Reformed doctrine of perseverance rather than against it. Jude is not describing believers who lost salvation; the whole letter distinguishes these men from the beloved who are preserved in Jesus Christ (Jude 1:1) and closes with the doxology to Him who is able to keep us from falling. They are men who crept in unawares, who feasted with the church without fear, and whose fruitlessness was finally exposed. 1 John 2:19 states the principle plainly: they went out from us, but they were not of us. The tree that is plucked up by the roots is shown never to have been rooted.
roots_summary: Greek dis (G1364), twice; apothnesko (G599), to die; ekrizoo (G1610), to root out; Hebrew paamayim, two times.
roots_lines: Greek dis (G1364) — twice; twice dead (Jude 1:12) and the Pharisee’s twice in the week (Luke 18:12).
Greek ekrizoo (G1610) — to uproot, to pluck up by the roots; the second half of Jude’s image.
Greek phthinoporinos (G5352) — of late autumn, when fruit should be present and is not; trees whose fruit withereth.
Hebrew paamayim — two times, twice; God speaketh once, yea twice (Job 33:14).
Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn or return; the repeated warnings of 2 Kings 6:10.
usage: Twice dead, plucked up by the roots (Jude 1:12) — dead in sin, and dead again in abandoned profession.
God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not (Job 33:14) — the failure is in the perceiving.
I fast twice in the week (Luke 18:12) — a true record offered as a ground, and he went down unjustified.

etymology: From Latin punctum, a prick or small hole, from pungere, to prick. Webster 1828: the sharp end of anything; an indivisible part of space or time; a particular of a subject. James uses it for a single article of the law, and its breaking implicates the whole.
biblical_def: James states the unity of the law in a sentence that has troubled every reader who has tried to keep a selection of it: whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all (James 2:10). The law is not a list of separate requirements from which a passing score may be assembled; it is the will of one Lawgiver, and to break it anywhere is to have broken with Him. The word also marks extremity of time. Esau, back from the field and famished, uses it to justify a trade: Behold, I am at the point to die: and what profit shall this birthright do to me? (Genesis 25:32) — an exaggeration that let him despise a birthright for a meal, and Hebrews 12:16 calls him a profane person for it. Jairus uses the same phrase in earnest, and it is not an exaggeration: My little daughter lieth at the point of death: I pray thee, come and lay thy hands on her, that she may be healed; and she shall live (Mark 5:23) — and before Christ arrives she dies.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines POINT as the sharp end of any instrument; a small space; an indivisible part of time or space; a particular or single part of a subject; the precise moment or juncture.
webster_full: POINT, n. — The sharp end of any instrument or body; as the point of a sword.
An indivisible part of space or time; a mark of position.
A particular; a single part or article of a subject; as, to answer every point.
The precise moment or juncture; as, at the point of death.
Latin punctum, from pungo, to prick — the root of puncture, punctual, pungent.
scriptures: James 2:10
For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.
Genesis 25:32
And Esau said, Behold, I am at the point to die: and what profit shall this birthright do to me?
Mark 5:23
And besought him greatly, saying, My little daughter lieth at the point of death: I pray thee, come and lay thy hands on her, that she may be healed; and she shall live.
James 2:11
For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now if thou commit no adultery, yet if thou kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law.
corruption_summary: James 2:10 destroys the ledger view of morality in which good deeds are weighed against bad, and with it every religion of net balance, including the folk version most people actually hold.
corruption_paragraphs: Whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all. James gives the reason in the next verse: the same God who forbade adultery forbade killing, so the transgression of any command is a transgression against the one Lawgiver. This dismantles the ledger — the intuition, nearly universal and quite unbiblical, that a man’s good deeds may be set against his bad and the balance struck. Rome’s system of merit, satisfaction and purgatory is the developed form of the error, but the folk version is more common and more dangerous, since most people who have never opened a catechism nonetheless assume it. Against it stands the Reformed doctrine of justification: the law demands perfect obedience, no sinner supplies it, and the righteousness by which a man is accepted is Christ’s, imputed and received by faith alone.

Esau’s I am at the point to die is worth setting beside Jairus’s use of the same phrase, because one man was exaggerating and the other was not. Esau was hungry after a day’s hunting, in his father’s camp, surrounded by flocks; he was not dying, and Hebrews 12:16 names him a profane person who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. The mechanism is instructive — a present appetite dramatized into an emergency, so that a permanent thing may be traded for an immediate one. Jairus was not exaggerating, and his daughter died before Christ reached the house. The contrast is between a man who invented urgency to justify what he wanted and a man whose real extremity was met, after a delay, with Be not afraid, only believe.
roots_summary: Greek en heni, in one thing; eschatos echo, to be at the last extremity; Hebrew halak lamuth, going to die; Latin punctum, a prick.
roots_lines: Greek en heni — in one point or particular; offend in one point (James 2:10).
Greek ptaio (G4417) — to stumble or trip; the verb rendered offend in the same verse.
Greek eschatos echei — literally hath it at the last; lieth at the point of death (Mark 5:23).
Hebrew halak lamuth — going to die; Esau’s claim in Genesis 25:32.
Greek parabates (G3848) — a transgressor, one who steps across a line (James 2:11).
usage: Offend in one point, he is guilty of all (James 2:10) — the law is one Lawgiver’s will, not a list to score.
Behold, I am at the point to die (Genesis 25:32) — an appetite dramatized into an emergency.
My little daughter lieth at the point of death (Mark 5:23) — a real extremity, met after a delay.
